title: Organisational capacity: Technology purchases cannot deliver transition
desc: Treats reskilling, redeployment, working conditions and public support as complements to automation, with substantial sector heterogeneity.

kps.k: Workforce and organisational capacity, not technology acquisition alone, constrain transformation.
kps.d: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 frames adaptation through employers’ 2024 expectations for 2025–2030. Skills gaps lead perceived barriers at 63%, ranking first in 52 of 55 economies and 19 of 22 sectors. Employers also cite cultural resistance (46%), regulatory frameworks (39%) and inadequate data and technical infrastructure (32%). The practical implication is to pair technology investment with skills development and changes to processes, structures and management practices. These findings measure perceived constraints, not their demonstrated causal effects.

kps.k: Employers anticipate automation alongside human–technology collaboration, rather than a simple substitution of machines for workers.
kps.d: The report’s global task allocation shifts from 48% predominantly human, 30% combined and 22% predominantly technological work to 33%, 33% and 34% respectively by 2030. Employers plan workforce upskilling (85%), accelerated automation (73%) and technological augmentation (63%). These overlapping strategies accommodate both substitution and augmentation. Task shares do not measure jobs lost, and intentions do not establish realised productivity or employment effects.

kps.k: Reskilling and redeployment anchor the proposed workforce response, but successful transitions remain unproven.
kps.d: For AI specifically, 77% of employers plan to reskill existing workers, 69% to hire people who can design AI tools and 62% to hire people who can work alongside AI; 47% plan internal transitions from jobs expected to decline because of AI. The broader training outlook assigns 29 of every 100 workers to upskilling in their current roles, 19 to upskilling and redeployment, and 11 to being unlikely to upskill. Employers expect productivity, competitiveness and retention gains, but the survey does not measure those returns. The tension is between ambitious adaptation plans and an anticipated group that training will not reach.

kps.k: Employer priorities vary by sector and economy; the evidence shows heterogeneity rather than a direct dispute between sources.
kps.d: Skills gaps dominate globally, but healthcare respondents cite cultural resistance more often than skills gaps, at 59% versus 46%. Projected task mixes also differ: information and technology services expects 26% predominantly human work in 2030, compared with 42% in real estate. Policy preferences reflect local circumstances: South African respondents emphasise training funding and education improvements, while Slovenian respondents prioritise hiring and firing flexibility. These differences qualify any uniform workforce prescription; they do not demonstrate which intervention works best.

kps.k: Training forms part of a wider talent strategy that includes working conditions, recruitment and public support.
kps.d: Employers identify well-being (64%), effective reskilling (63%), progression (62%), higher wages (50%) and broader talent pools (47%) as promising ways to improve talent availability. Public-policy preferences similarly emphasise reskilling funding (55%), training provision (52%) and education improvements (47%). This places responsibility for adaptation across employers and public institutions rather than on workers alone. The figures rank respondents’ preferences, not independently evaluated policy recommendations or intervention effects.

kps.k: The report supplies broad workforce context, not a legal-sector forecast or a clean measure of AI displacement.
kps.d: Employers anticipate transformation from AI alongside economic, demographic, climate and geopolitical pressures. The professional-services profile reports 95% running AI programmes, 41% core-skill disruption and 19% five-year labour-force churn, but these are distinct indicators and do not isolate legal services or AI-caused job losses. Likewise, the wage outlook measures compensation as a share of company revenue, not individual wage changes. Truncated labels and anomalous profile values warrant caution when interpreting individual statistics.

vlens.an: The supplied market-analysis source supports the proposition that technology purchases alone cannot deliver organisational transition. The Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies skills gaps, organisational resistance, regulation and infrastructure as material constraints, and reports employer plans that combine automation with upskilling, augmentation, specialist hiring and redeployment. It also supports the proposition’s broader distribution of responsibility through attention to working conditions, recruitment and public reskilling support. Material internal variation qualifies rather than contradicts this position: sectors differ in their leading barriers and expected human–technology task mix, while economies prioritise different policy responses. The evidence is also limited to surveyed employers’ 2024 expectations and intentions for 2025–2030; it does not demonstrate that these interventions will succeed or establish realised employment effects. As only one curated source represents this professional voice here, no inference about prevalence across market analysts, consultancies or the press is warranted.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that technology purchases alone cannot deliver organisational transition. Based on employers’ 2024 survey responses about 2025–2030, it identifies skills gaps, cultural resistance, regulatory constraints and inadequate infrastructure as barriers, and presents upskilling, augmentation, recruitment and redeployment as complements to automation. Material variation qualifies rather than undermines that support: healthcare respondents prioritise cultural resistance over skills gaps; projected human–technology task mixes differ across sectors; and preferred public interventions vary by economy. The evidence is also limited to reported expectations and plans—not realised transition outcomes, causal effects or a legal-sector-specific forecast. Because the corpus contains a curated source rather than a representative survey of published viewpoints, its position should not be treated as indicating wider prevalence.
